questions.prompt: A container runs as root with Docker's defaults and mounts `/var/run/docker.sock` read-only "for metrics". An attacker gets a shell inside it. How far can they get?
choices: Only the container: the socket is mounted read-only
The container and its volumes
The whole host: the socket is the Docker API with root privileges, a read-only bind mount does not stop connect(), and one API call starts a privileged container with / mounted
Nowhere: the default seccomp profile blocks access to unix sockets
questions.explanation: A read-only mount affects open() for writing, not connecting to a socket. Anything that can talk to the Docker API can create a container with --privileged and the host root bind-mounted, which is root on the host. No flag on the compromised container matters once that mount exists; remove it or put a socket proxy with an allow-list in front.

questions.prompt: In Docker's default seccomp profile, `mount`, `unshare`, `setns` and `bpf` sit in a rule with `includes: {caps: [CAP_SYS_ADMIN]}`. What does `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` change?
choices: Two things at once: the process gains the capability bit and the seccomp filter built for it now allows mount, unshare, setns, bpf and the rest of that rule
Only the capability bit; the filter is compiled once when the daemon starts
Nothing unless --privileged is also set
It disables seccomp for that container
questions.explanation: The daemon resolves the profile per container against the container's bounding set: rules whose includes.caps are satisfied become part of the filter. Adding a capability therefore also widens the syscall filter, which is why hardencheck reports mount as "ERRNO, allowed with CAP_SYS_ADMIN" and why SYS_ADMIN is never just one bit.

questions.prompt: You generate a profile from `strace -f python3 -c print` on your Ubuntu laptop and run `python:3.12-alpine` under it. The container fails to start. Most likely cause?
choices: Alpine images need --privileged to accept custom profiles
The profile must list architectures or the daemon rejects it
Custom profiles only work with seccompProfile type RuntimeDefault
The trace shows glibc's loader and libc; the image uses musl, which makes different syscalls, so the profile denies calls the image needs. Trace inside the image the profile is for.
questions.explanation: A profile is an allow-list of what one binary and one libc do. glibc uses newfstatat, rseq and statx where musl uses fstat, open and stat; a different Python build and version add more differences. Trace the exact image (apk add strace inside it), then run that image under the result.

questions.prompt: A Deployment's pod template sets `runAsNonRoot: true` and `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` at pod level. One container sets `seccompProfile.type: Unconfined` and `runAsUser: 0`. What does a namespace with `enforce=restricted` do with it?
choices: Admits it: pod-level settings take precedence
Rejects it: container-level settings override pod-level ones, Unconfined and runAsUser 0 are forbidden, and every container must also set allowPrivilegeEscalation false and drop ALL
Admits it with a warning because runAsNonRoot is set
Rejects it only if the audit label is also present
questions.explanation: A container's securityContext overrides the pod's for the fields it sets. The restricted standard checks the effective value per container: Unconfined seccomp and runAsUser 0 are violations, and allowPrivilegeEscalation=false and capabilities.drop=[ALL] have no pod-level form, so each container must state them. Enforcement rejects at admission regardless of the warn and audit labels.

questions.prompt: You want a seccomp allow-list for a service with a large test suite, but a missed syscall in production would be an outage. What is the safe path?
choices: Ship with SCMP_ACT_KILL_PROCESS and watch for crashes
There is none; run seccomp=unconfined

Generate from a trace, set defaultAction to SCMP_ACT_LOG, run the test suite and staging under it, collect unlisted syscalls from the kernel log (dmesg or journalctl -k), add them, then switch the default to SCMP_ACT_ERRNO
Use RuntimeDefault; custom profiles cannot be audited
questions.explanation: SCMP_ACT_LOG records every syscall the rules do not match without denying it, so a profile can be grown against real traffic before it is enforced. Kubernetes exposes the same idea through a Localhost profile with a logging default action. Only when the log stays quiet do you flip the default to ERRNO.

questions.prompt: Your pod is admitted under `enforce=restricted`. Which of these is still true unless you add it yourself?
choices: The root filesystem is writable, there is no memory limit and the service account token is mounted: restricted does not require readOnlyRootFilesystem, resources.limits or automountServiceAccountToken: false
The container may still run as root
Privilege escalation through setuid binaries is still possible
The pod may still mount a hostPath volume
questions.explanation: Restricted guarantees non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, a seccomp profile and safe volume types. It says nothing about a writable root filesystem, resource limits or the API credential every pod gets by default, which is why hardencheck reports those three as "extra" and why the runbook adds them anyway.
